transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic?

Hi, Doctor. Well, um, I guess I'm here because... honestly, things have been getting really weird lately, especially at my job. I work as a bookkeeping clerk—I got the job right out of high school, and it's usually pretty straightforward, just a lot of data entry and reconciling accounts. But recently, I've started doing these things at work, and even at my night classes, that just... they just do not make any sense at all. 

Like, the other day, instead of entering the travel expenses into the system, I took all the physical receipts for the whole month and just started lining them up across the floor. I don't even really know why, I just felt like I had to get them in this perfect, straight line stretching all the way from my desk down the hall. It took me so long to do it, too. And then there's my calculator. I use a 10-key a lot, obviously, but I've started doing this thing where I just tap the keys, but it has to be in exact sets of nine. Tap, tap, tap... just nine times, over and over. If I lose count, I have to clear it and start the nine taps all over again, not even doing math, just tapping. 

And it's not just at my desk, either. I'll go to the copy machine to scan some invoices, and instead of hitting start, I'll just stand there with my hands held up in the air, like, right up by my head, and I just freeze. I'll stay like that, just staring at the wall behind the machine, until somebody walks by and asks if I am okay. It's only when they ask that I realize how strange it looks, and it's so embarrassing, but I just... I don't know why I keep doing this stuff.

When you feel the urge to do these things—like lining up the receipts or tapping the keys nine times—do you feel like you're being forced to do them against your will, or does it feel more natural, like it's just what you want to do?

That’s... gosh, that’s a really hard question, actually. I don't really know if I can say it's either of those things. It’s not like I’m being forced, you know? Like, there’s nobody holding a gun to my head or grabbing my hands and making me press the keys on the 10-key. And I don’t feel this big, scary pressure like 'do this or else something terrible will happen.' But at the same time, I wouldn't say it feels natural, either, because I definitely don't actually want to be doing it. 

Like, when you want to do something, you usually have a reason, right? Like if I want to go down the hall to the breakroom to get a coffee—we just got one of those new Keurig machines last month, the ones with the little touchscreen—I know I’m doing it because I’m tired and I want the caffeine to get through the afternoon. But with the receipts... I remember holding that big stack of them, and they have that weird, smooth thermal paper texture that leaves a residue on your fingers if you hold them too long, and I just... I really don't know. I didn't plan it. I didn't think, 'Oh, it would be great to line these up right now instead of doing my job.' I just sort of found myself doing it. 

It’s almost like my brain just goes completely blank and the next thing I know, I'm down on the office carpet making sure the edges of the papers are perfectly parallel. So I really can't tell you if it's my will or not. I've actually spent hours just sitting on my couch at home after my night classes, just staring up at the ceiling, trying to retrace my steps and figure out if I actually chose to put those receipts on the floor or if I chose to tap that calculator nine times. And I just can't come up with an answer. It’s just this big, confusing blank space where my normal decision-making should be. I don't know if that makes any sense at all, but I just can't figure out where the urge even comes from.

When you're doing these things—like lining up the receipts or tapping the keys—do you have thoughts or worries running through your head at the time, or does it feel more like your body is just doing it on its own without much thinking involved?

Well, that's... that's the thing that really bothers me about it, honestly. Because, like I said, when I try to think back on it, my mind is just... it's just blank. So, no, I don't really have any worries or, you know, specific thoughts running through my head when I'm doing it. It's not like I'm thinking, 'Oh, if I don't tap this nine times, my boss is going to fire me,' or 'If these receipts aren't perfectly straight, the company will go bankrupt.' There's none of that. It's just... quiet up there. 

And I know that sounds crazy, because how can you just do something for that long and not be thinking about anything? But it really does feel like my body is just... going on autopilot, almost. Like the time with the copy machine, when I just froze with my hands up. I wasn't standing there worrying about the toner running low or thinking about my night class assignment that was due the next day. I was just... there. Just existing, in that weird pose, staring at the beige wall. I think they painted it that color to look professional, but it just looks kind of depressing, you know? Anyway, yeah, I wasn't thinking about the wall, either. 

It's so frustrating because I feel like if I was worrying about something, at least I could point to it and say, 'Okay, I did this weird thing because I was stressed about X, Y, or Z.' But without any thoughts attached to it, it just feels like my body is glitching out or something. Like a computer program that just gets stuck in a loop for no reason. I don't know, it's just really unsettling to not be in the driver's seat of your own actions, even when your mind isn't busy with anything else.

Before you start doing these things—like before you line up the receipts or freeze at the copy machine—do you ever notice that a particular thought or image pops into your head that feels uncomfortable or wrong, even if just for a second?

Well, I’ve... I’ve actually tried to think about that too, because like I said, I spend all that time just sitting on my couch trying to rewind the tape of my day to figure out what went wrong. I’ll think, okay, I was walking to the copier. And our copier is this massive, industrial Canon machine, it hums really loud all day and the second paper tray always gets jammed if you don't load the ream exactly right. So I try to put myself right back in that exact moment before I froze, just to see if I missed something. 

But no, there’s no... there's no flash of anything bad or uncomfortable. It’s not like I see a scary picture in my head or have a sudden weird thought that I need to push away or anything like that. 

Like, right before I lined up all those travel receipts... I was just sitting at my desk. I remember I had just finished my lunch—it was a turkey and swiss on rye from the deli across the street, they always put a little too much mayo on it, but it’s cheap so I go there a lot—and I was just looking at the stack of thermal paper. There wasn’t any image popping into my brain. No sudden uncomfortable feeling or wrong thought. It’s literally just... nothing. One second I’m just a normal guy sitting at his desk digesting his sandwich and looking at an expense report, and the next second I’m down on the floor making a paper trail down the hallway. 

And with the copy machine, it was the exact same thing. I was walking down the hall, just looking at the floor—it’s that weird blue and gray speckled carpet that every corporate office has because it hides coffee stains really well—and I got to the machine. No weird thoughts, no bad images flashing before my eyes, no sudden panic. I just lifted my hands up and froze. I mean, I really wish there was a thought, honestly. It would make so much more sense to me if I could tell you, 'Yeah, Doc, I had this horrible image of a car crash pop into my head, so I froze to try and make it go away.' But there is just absolutely nothing. Just this huge, empty gap right where a thought or a reason is supposed to be. It makes me feel like I’m losing my grip, but not in a way where my mind is full of crazy stuff... just in a way where it’s totally empty right before I do these things. So no, I haven't noticed anything like that at all.

Looking back to when you were a kid—say, in elementary school or middle school—did you ever have any habits or things you liked to do over and over again in a particular way, like lining things up, organizing things, or repeating actions a certain number of times?

Gosh, thinking back to when I was a kid... you know, elementary school, middle school. I actually went to this really small elementary school, Oak Creek Elementary, and it was one of those older brick buildings with the really high windows where the teachers always had to use a long wooden pole with a metal hook on the end to pull them open when the AC broke, which was basically all the time in September. But anyway, no, I really didn't do anything like that back then. Honestly, I was probably the exact opposite of organized. 

My mom used to get so incredibly frustrated with me because my bedroom was just a total disaster zone. I had this huge plastic bin of Legos—just the standard assorted blocks, not the fancy kits they have now where you build a whole movie scene with instructions, just the random bricks—and I never lined them up or sorted them by color or size or anything like that. I would just dump them all over that cheap green shag carpet we had and leave them there. She was always stepping on them in her bare feet and yelling at me to clean it up. 

And it was the exact same way with my school stuff. By the time I got to middle school, my locker was just this terrifying black hole of crumpled up worksheets and old gym clothes. I remember once I found a half-eaten sandwich in there from like three weeks prior, wrapped in one of those crinkly plastic ziplock bags, just shoved all the way in the back behind my math textbook. 

So, yeah, I definitely didn't have any habits where I had to do things a certain number of times or keep things perfectly straight. I was just a really typical, messy kid who wanted to ride his bike and play video games until dinner. I never tapped things or felt the need to organize my toys in a row or anything even close to that. All this weird stuff with the receipts and the copy machine and the numbers... it's all completely new to me. It definitely didn't start back then. I was just a regular, disorganized kid.

When you're around other people at work or in your night classes, do you ever feel like you have trouble understanding what they're thinking or feeling, or like you're not quite on the same wavelength socially? Or have people ever told you that you come across as a bit odd or different in the way you interact with them?

No, not at all, actually. I mean, I feel like I'm pretty good at reading people, you know? Like at work, I sit in this pod of four cubicles—they’re those really low-walled ones that are supposed to encourage 'collaboration' but really just mean you can hear every single time someone crunches on a potato chip or clears their throat—and I get along with everyone just fine. I feel like I know exactly what they're feeling most of the time. Like my supervisor, Dave, he’s this older guy who always wears these slightly wrinkled blue button-downs, and I can always tell when he’s stressed about the month-end close because he starts clicking his pen, just click-click-click, and his posture gets totally rigid. I don't have any trouble understanding that he needs space when he gets like that, so I just hand him the reconciliation reports and back away. We joke around a lot on normal days, too, mostly about baseball or how terrible the breakroom coffee is. Nobody has ever pulled me aside or said I'm acting weird in conversations or missing social cues or anything like that. 

And it's the exact same thing in my night classes. I'm taking this Intro to Managerial Accounting class on Tuesday and Thursday nights at the community college—which is honestly exhausting after staring at numbers all day, and the fluorescent lights in that specific lecture hall just completely drain whatever energy you have left by 7 PM—but socially, I'm totally on the same wavelength as everyone else there. We actually had this group project a couple of weeks ago where we had to do a mock cost analysis, and I was the one who kind of had to read the room and mediate because these two girls in my group were getting really annoyed with each other over who was going to format the final Excel spreadsheet. I could totally pick up on their passive-aggressive vibes, you know, the heavy sighing and the really tight, fake smiles they were giving each other, so I just stepped in and offered to do the formatting myself to smooth things over. I understood exactly what was happening there.

So, yeah, I definitely don't feel disconnected from people or like I don't understand what they're thinking. I mean, obviously, if they actually saw me freezing at the copy machine or doing the weird thing with the receipts on the floor, I'm sure they'd think *that* was incredibly bizarre. Who wouldn't? But just talking to me? Interacting with me day to day at my desk or before class starts? No, I'm just a regular guy. I can read a room perfectly fine, and I've never had anyone tell me I'm odd to talk to or that I don't get what's going on socially.

When you're doing these things—like the tapping or the freezing—does it feel like something inside you gets relieved or feels 'complete' once you finish? Or does stopping these behaviors feel uncomfortable in any way, like something is left undone?

You know, I... I’ve actually thought about that exact thing, because you see it in movies, right? Like someone has to flip a light switch ten times or wash their hands a bunch, and then they let out this big sigh of relief because they finally finished doing it and they feel safe or whatever. But for me... no. No, it doesn’t feel like that at all. There’s absolutely no sense of relief. It doesn't feel like I accomplished anything or like some internal pressure valve got released. 

Like with the tapping. The other day I was at my desk—it's this really cheap fake mahogany laminate desk that management bought in bulk a few years ago, and the edge where my wrists rest is all chipped away so it actually scratches your forearms if you're not careful—and I was doing that tapping thing with my knuckles against the side of the filing drawer. And my supervisor, Dave, the guy I mentioned earlier with the wrinkly shirts, he walked over to my cubicle to ask me if I had pulled the vendor invoices for the quarterly tax prep. And when he walked up and said my name, I just... stopped. I didn't feel this overwhelming, horrible urge to go back and finish tapping. It didn't feel like I left a sentence half-finished or like my skin was crawling because I didn't get to do it a certain number of times. I didn't feel uncomfortable at all. I just stopped tapping, turned around in my swivel chair, and handed him the manila folder with the invoices. 

And it’s the exact same way with the freezing at the copy machine. When I finally snap out of it and put my hands down, I don't feel like, 'Ah, great, I did it, I'm good now.' I don't feel complete. If anything, I just feel incredibly confused and, honestly, a little embarrassed. I just look at the massive Canon machine, and I look at the paper tray, and I realize I've just been standing there like a store mannequin for absolutely no reason. There’s no payoff to it. It’s not scratching an itch. So, yeah, stopping doesn't bother me at all, and finishing doesn't make me feel better. It’s just... it just happens, and then it’s over, and I'm left sitting there trying to figure out why I just wasted my time doing it.

When you freeze at the copy machine with your hands held up in the air, are you still aware of what's happening around you—like if someone called your name or walked by—or does it feel like time kind of disappears and you're not really aware of anything until someone actually interrupts you?

You know, it's really strange when you put it like that, because... well, I am aware, but also kind of not? It's hard to explain. Like, I came in to see you because I've started doing all these things at work and school that just completely do not make sense. Like I mentioned before, the lining the receipts up across the floor—which, by the way, is incredibly unsanitary because the cleaning crew at my office building is practically non-existent and they only vacuum maybe once every two weeks, so the carpet is always covered in dust and little paper punches from the three-hole puncher. And then there's the tapping the calculator in sets of nine, which I do right at my desk, just tap-tap-tap, over and over. And then, of course, standing by the copier with my hands held up. 

When I'm doing that copier thing... I mean, the machine is this huge, loud thing, right? It hums, and you can hear the paper feeding through the trays, and the fluorescent lights in the copy room are always buzzing. So I hear all of that. I know I'm standing there. But I just... I hold my hands up in the air, almost like I'm surrendering to the machine or something ridiculous like that, and I just stay like that. I don't really know how much time is passing. It could be ten seconds, it could be two minutes. I'm just frozen there. 

And I'll just stay like that until someone actually walks in and asks if I'm okay. Like last week, Brenda from Human Resources—she always wears these really strong floral perfumes that you can smell from down the hall before you even see her—she walked in to get her 1099 forms printed, and she just stopped and stared at me. She was like, 'Are you alright?' And the second she said it, it was like a spell broke or something. I just put my hands down, grabbed my papers, and mumbled something about static electricity. But until she actually spoke to me, I was just... stuck. I knew I was there, but I couldn't really snap myself out of it until she interrupted me. It’s just so bizarre, honestly. I don't know why I'm doing any of this stuff.

During these episodes—like when you're frozen at the copy machine or lining up the receipts—do you feel disconnected from your own body, like you're watching yourself from the outside, or does it feel more like your body is just moving on its own while your mind stays present?

No, it’s not really like that. I mean, I’ve heard of people describing things like that, like an out-of-body experience where you’re floating up by the ceiling and watching yourself, but I definitely don’t have that. When I’m down on the floor lining up those receipts—and like I said, those are the really cheap thermal paper receipts, the kind that fade completely if you leave them on your car dashboard and they leave this weird, slick chemical residue on your fingertips if you handle too many of them at once—I am very much in my own body. I can feel the rough, dirty carpet on my knees, I can feel the paper on my fingers, I’m looking through my own eyes. I’m not hovering above myself or disconnected from reality in that way. 

And as for my body moving on its own... no, not that either. It doesn't feel like I'm a puppet on strings or like I'm just a passenger in my own head watching my hands do things without my permission. I know I'm the one moving my hands. Like with the copier, when I have my hands up in the air, I can actually feel the strain in my shoulders starting to build up, because holding your arms up like that completely still for even just a minute gets surprisingly tiring, especially since I don't really lift weights or anything, I mostly just carry boxes of printer paper or ledger binders around the office. So I feel the muscle tension, I feel my feet in my shoes, I know I'm the one holding my arms up. I'm completely present in my physical body. 

It’s just... I don't know, it's just that I'm doing these things and I don't have a logical reason for *why* I'm doing them. But I'm definitely the one doing them. I'm not disconnected at all. I'm just stuck doing something completely illogical until the moment passes or someone like Brenda interrupts me. So, yeah, no floating outside my body or feeling like a robot whose programming took over. Just me, in my body, doing weird stuff for absolutely no reason.

When you're doing these things—like lining up the receipts or tapping the calculator—do you ever lose track of time in a way where you can't quite remember what happened, or does it feel like you were there the whole time but just don't know why you were doing it?

No, I don't... I don't lose track of time like that. I mean, I don't black out or anything. It's actually kind of the exact opposite. I am painfully aware of every single second that passes, and I remember everything. 

Like, take the calculator tapping. I use this heavy-duty Casio printing calculator at my desk—it’s one of those older, bulky models that takes the standard two-and-a-quarter inch paper rolls, and it has the two-color ink ribbon so all the negative numbers print out in this really sharp red ink, which is honestly super helpful when I'm reconciling the daily ledger because you can spot a discrepancy a mile away. Anyway, when I'm tapping the side of it in those sets of nine, I am totally there. I can feel the hard plastic of the casing, I can hear the little mechanical sound it makes when my knuckles hit it, and I can literally see the clock on the wall right above Dave's cubicle. It's this cheap plastic wall clock, the kind you'd see in a high school math classroom, and the second hand makes this really distinct, annoying ticking sound that you can only hear when the HVAC system kicks off. 

So I'm sitting there, doing the tapping, and I can watch that red second hand move tick by tick. I know exactly how much time is passing. I remember the whole thing from start to finish. It's not like a blackout or amnesia or whatever happens to people on those medical TV shows where they wake up in a different room and don't know how they got there. 

So, yeah, it's exactly what you said at the end there. I'm there the whole time. I remember everything I did. I just... I just don't have the faintest clue *why* I was doing it. I'll finish lining up those receipts—and like I said, my fingers will be all gross and slick from the thermal coating they put on that paper—and I'll look at this perfectly straight line of receipts on the dirty carpet, and I'll just think, 'Okay, well, that was completely pointless.' But I remember doing it. Every agonizing second of it. I just don't understand what the point of any of it is.

Even though you've said there's no specific thought or worry triggering these behaviors, when you're doing them—like the tapping or the freezing—do you feel any sense of anxiety, dread, or like something is wrong, even if you can't quite put your finger on what it is?

Anxiety? Or dread? Um... no, not really. And I know I keep repeating myself, but that's honestly the exact reason I came in to see you in the first place. Because I’ve started doing all these bizarre things at work, and at school too—I take a couple of evening classes at the community college, just trying to get my associate's degree in accounting so I can eventually move up from being a bookkeeping clerk to maybe a real staff accountant someday, because the pay bump is pretty significant and you actually get decent health insurance. But anyway, I've started doing these things at work and school that just absolutely do not make any sense whatsoever, and there's no emotional reason behind them. 

There's no feeling of doom or like... like my heart is racing or I'm sweating because something terrible is about to happen. I'm not worried about anything specific at all. It's just... suddenly I'm down on the floor lining up those awful thermal receipts, or I'm sitting in the middle of my tax law lecture or at my office desk tapping that calculator in sets of nine, or I'm just standing there by the copy machine with my hands held straight up in the air until someone finally walks by and asks if I am okay. 

While it's happening, I don't feel scared. I don't feel anxious or like something is wrong. It's almost like my brain just decides, okay, this is what we are doing right now, and I just do it. It’s only afterward, or when someone like Brenda actually interrupts me and breaks the spell, that I feel weird about it, because I look at what I'm doing and realize it's completely irrational. But during it? No, no dread or panic at all. Just... doing things that make zero sense for no apparent reason.

If you really tried hard—say, if your job depended on it—do you think you could stop yourself from doing these things, like the tapping or the freezing, or would it feel impossible to hold back even if you wanted to?

Could I stop myself? That’s... that’s a really tough question, actually. Because, you see, to stop yourself from doing something, you usually have to feel the urge coming on, right? Like, if you have a bad cough, you feel that little tickle in the back of your throat, and if you're in a quiet meeting or taking a test, you can maybe hold your breath, drink some water, and suppress it for a minute. You know it's coming, so you can fight it. 

But with this... well, I know I keep coming back to this, but it really is the entire reason I came in to see you in the first place—because I have started doing things at work and school that do not make sense, like lining receipts across the floor, tapping the calculator in sets of nine, or standing by the copier with my hands held up until someone asks if I am okay. And the thing is, I don't plan to do any of it. There's no warning tickle in my brain. 

If my job depended on it... man, I mean, I really, really need this job. It pays for my evening classes at the community college, and my car insurance actually just went up because I had a minor fender bender in the parking lot of the grocery store last month—which was totally not my fault, the other guy just backed out of his spot without even looking in his rearview mirror, but my rates still went up anyway. So I absolutely *need* this paycheck. If my supervisor, Mr. Abernathy, came up to my desk and said, 'Listen, if you do that weird thing with the thermal receipts one more time, you're fired,' I would desperately *want* to stop. I would try with everything I have. 

But honestly? I don't think I could. Because I don't know I'm about to do it until I'm already doing it. It's not like I'm sitting at my desk looking at the Casio calculator and thinking, 'Oh, I have a really strong urge to tap this right now, but I better hold back so Mr. Abernathy doesn't fire me.' It doesn't work like that. I just suddenly find myself doing it. So even if my job was on the line, or if I was in the middle of a huge, heavily weighted final exam for my tax law class and I really needed to focus on the paper in front of me, I don't think I could just 'hold back.' It feels impossible to prevent because there's no buildup. I just start doing it, and then I'm stuck in it, perfectly aware of what I'm doing, until someone interrupts me or it just randomly stops.

Right before you start doing one of these things—like just a split second before you tap the calculator or freeze at the copy machine—do you ever feel a tingling, tension, or uncomfortable sensation anywhere in your body, like an itch you need to scratch or a buildup of pressure that gets released once you do the behavior?

A tingling? Like an itch? No... no, I don't feel anything like that at all. I mean, I know what physical tension feels like, believe me. I sit in this terribly cheap, supposedly ergonomic mesh chair at the office for eight hours a day, and I get this awful knot right between my shoulder blades, usually right around 3:00 PM every day, and I have to kind of twist in my seat to crack my back. So I know what a buildup of pressure feels like, and I know what that release feels like when you finally stretch it out and hear that pop. 

But this isn't like that. Not even close. Like I keep saying—and I know I probably sound like a broken record today, I'm sorry, I really don't mean to keep circling back, it's just that this is the entire reason I made this appointment in the first place. I came in because I have started doing things at work and school that do not make sense, like lining receipts across the floor, tapping the calculator in sets of nine, or standing by the copier with my hands held up until someone asks if I am okay. And before any of that happens, my body feels completely, one hundred percent normal. 

There's no itch. There's no tingling in my fingers before I start tapping the keys on the Casio. There's no weird tension in my shoulders before my arms go up at the copier. Like, last Tuesday, I was actually just trying to print out the quarterly tax summaries for Mr. Abernathy, and the machine was doing that annoying calibration thing it does where it hums and whirs for like two minutes straight before it even grabs the first piece of paper, and then suddenly my hands are just up in the air. I didn't feel a tickle in my muscles, I didn't feel a sudden physical urge, and I definitely didn't feel any sense of relief or release once they were up there. It's not like scratching a mosquito bite. It's purely just... one second I'm waiting for my copies, and the next second I'm doing the weird thing, and my body feels exactly the same the whole time.

When you're frozen at the copy machine with your hands held up in the air, if someone gently tried to move your arm down or reposition it, would your arm move easily, or would it feel stiff and resistant, like it wants to stay in that exact position?

That's... well, I actually know the answer to that one, because it happened just last week. Brenda, the office manager—she's this older lady, always wears these brightly colored floral blouses and brings in awful stale donuts on Fridays—anyway, she walked by while I was doing it. I was just standing there, hands straight up in the air, right next to the big Xerox machine. It was doing that loud humming thing, and I was just... stuck. 

She walked over, looking really confused, and she said my name a couple of times. When I didn't answer right away, she actually reached out and kind of pushed on my elbow, like she was trying to get me to lower my arm. And... it was weird. My arm just stayed there. It wasn't like I was flexing my muscles or trying to fight her on purpose, but it felt stiff, like... like my arm had turned into a heavy piece of wood or something. It didn't just drop down easily. She actually had to put a little bit of force into it, and even then, it felt like my arm wanted to spring right back up into that exact same awkward position. 

It was so embarrassing. She asked me what on earth I was doing, and I didn't have an answer for her. Which, honestly, is exactly why I'm sitting here talking to you today. I know I've said it a million times, but I really only came in because I have started doing all these bizarre things at work and school that just absolutely do not make any sense whatsoever. The receipts on the floor, the tapping the calculator exactly nine times, standing by the copier with my hands up in the air like I'm being robbed until someone finally notices and asks if I'm okay... none of it makes sense. And when Brenda tried to move my arm, it just felt totally locked in place. It wasn't until she really kind of shook me and broke the spell that I could finally put my hands down and act normal again.

When Brenda pushed your arm down from that position at the copy machine, after she moved it down, did your arm stay down in whatever position she left it in, or did it want to go back up to that same raised position?

Well, like I was saying before, it really wanted to go right back up. When she first pushed my arm down, it felt exactly like a spring. You know those cheap desk lamps where if you bend the neck but you forget to tighten the little screw, it just slowly creeps right back up to where it was? It was exactly like that. Brenda pushed my elbow down, but as soon as she let up the pressure even a little bit, my arm started drifting right back up toward the ceiling. It definitely did not just stay down where she left it. She had to literally shake my shoulder, like physically jostle me, and call my name really loudly before the whole weird spell finally broke and my arm relaxed. 

And once it broke, I was just so incredibly mortified. Because I am standing there thinking, why on earth am I doing this? Why can I not just be normal and do my job? I know I am probably driving you completely crazy repeating myself so much today, and I apologize for that, I really do, but I just cannot stress enough that this whole bizarre situation is the entire reason I made this appointment. I came in because I have started doing things at work and school that do not make sense, like lining receipts across the floor, tapping the calculator in sets of nine, or standing by the copier with my hands held up until someone asks if I am okay. 

I am a perfectly rational guy, I do bookkeeping, I work with numbers and spreadsheets, so everything is supposed to be organized and logical. But instead, I am doing all these things that completely disrupt my day. It is just so frustrating because none of it has any reason to it, and I just want to go back to doing my work and my accounting classes without all these bizarre interruptions.
